Marijuananews Note: I found this transcript in my files today, and I felt that I had to share it with everyone. Lester was a dear friend and he had a major impact on my life and on so many others. I also wanted to share with you the related stories from the MarijuanaNews files.

 

See Lester Grinspoon: The Forbidden Professor, RIP

And Dr. Grinspoon Asks, " Why won't the government let us use marijuana as medicine? " -- As UK Developer of " Water Soluble " Cannabis Says, " I would make cannabis available on the NHS now."

And The Nation Magazine Quotes Dr. Lester Grinspoon Explaining Why He Thinks Only Full Legalization Will Allow Proper Access to Medical Marijuana

And Dr. Lester Grinspoon Warns About The Pharmaceuticalization of Cannabis, As GW Pharmaceutical Hits All Time High After Deal With Bayer. But Does It Need Prohibition In Order to Succeed?

And Lester Grinspoon Attends Two Conferences On Medical Marijuana In Germany And Our Drug Czar Says that Medical Marijuana Is A Hoax To Legalize Drugs – Analysis Plus 2 Articles

 

“Good afternoon.  It's great to be at a NORML conference again, even if it's only a virtual presence.  I have been a part of these annual meetings since the first one in 1972. 

 

I had received a call from a young lawyer by the name of Keith Stroup who asked me to speak at the first annual conference of an organization he founded in 1970.  So I soon found myself in a rather dilapidated church in a seamy part of Washington standing in my three piece suit in front of perhaps three or four dozen very hip looking young people, when it struck me that it was absurd, almost, comical, that I, a marijuana virgin, should be lecturing to these folks who were clearly much more sophisticated about the subject than I. 

 

Well, I am glad to report to you that I have long since lost my virginity and I have become more sophisticated about marijuana. First, I will tell you a little  about how that came about.

 

In 1967, I would never have imagined that I would arrive at my present understanding of this drug. 

Marijuananews Note: That was the year that I began my own “research”, a work in progress.)

 

My enlightenment began that year when I found myself with some unexpected time because of a delay of about two months in getting some material I needed to finish my book on schizophrenia. 

 

Because I was so concerned about all of these foolish young people who were not taking seriously the government's dire warnings about the  health consequences of smoking marijuana, I decided to spend that time in the Countway library  with the goal of writing a review of the scientific literature upon which these alarming concerns were based. 

 

What I shortly discovered was my own abysmal ignorance about this drug, that despite my training in science and medicine I had been brainwashed like most Americans.  The resulting paper was published as the lead article in Scientific American, and the enormous interest it generated led to an invitation by Harvard University press to write a book on the subject. 

 

I decided to accept this invitation for two reasons: (1) it would provide me with both an opportunity to expand my knowledge of this fascinating drug and the almost universal cannabinophobic reaction to it, and (2) it was the only part of my work that my son, Danny, was interested in.  Danny was diagnosed as having acute lymphocytic leukemia in 1967.

 

The book, Marijuana Reconsidered, was published in 1971. 

 

I had concluded that marijuana was a remarkably non-toxic psychoactive substance and that the real harmfulness from its use resided, not in any inherent psychopharmacological property of the drug, but rather in the way we as a society we're dealing with it, that is by annually arresting, at that time about 300,000 mostly young people and criminalizing many more.  In the last chapter I predicted that the prohibition would be over within 10 years.  Interestingly, Carl Sagan, a close friend--- we would critically read each other's book manuscripts-- was delighted with the manuscript but certain that this estimate was mistaken, that I was being much too pessimistic, that the prohibition would surely be gone within a couple of years.

Marijuananews Note: Carl Sagan wrote an essay about his own experience with cannabis. See Marijuana Reconsidered

 

During my research for the book, just as I became increasingly convinced that its toxicity was quite limited, I also came to appreciate more and more that it apparently provided an experience that I wanted to personally explore.  But I decided not to try it at this time because I did not want to introduce a personal bias into what I was writing. 

 

Also, I correctly anticipated that if the book were successful, I would be asked to testify before various congressional committees, courts, commissions etc. and I wanted to able to honestly answer the question which would inevitably be asked, "Dr., have you ever smoked marijuana?”. 

 

At first, I had no problem with this question---it seemed to me a legitimate question about my qualifications.  But it soon became apparent that the person who asked the question was invariably hostile to my position.  It was during a hearing in 1973 that a senator who through his previous questions revealed his disdain for my position ,sure enough, asked this question. 

 

I replied, "Senator, I will be glad to answer your question, but would you first tell me if I answer affirmatively, would it, in your view, make me a more or less credible witness?" 

 

He stood up, pointed his finger at me and said, "You are being impertinent!" and he stormed out of the hearing room.  When I returned home that night, I said to Betsy, the time has come, and later that week at a party in Cambridge I ended my steadfastly held abstemiousness and from that time on my understanding of this fascinating drug began to be informed, not just by the scientific literature and anecdotal accounts, but by personal experience as well.

 

Over the 42 years since I began to study cannabis, my understanding of it has evolved considerably.  Whereas, when I first began my improbable involvement with marijuana, I believed it had only one use; now I believe that there are three broad, somewhat overlapping categories of usefulness: recreation, enhancement, and medicine. 

 

(1) Recreation.  I can be very brief about this because I believe there no people in this audience who do not understand from personal experience what a wonderful, safe, hangover- free recreational drug it is (well, undercover DEA agents have been known to attend this meeting).

 

(2) Enhancement. I believe that most people in this audience personally understand what I mean when I refer to this second category of usefulness which I call enhancement, the enhancement of a variety of personal experiences and capacities. 

 

Every user has experienced sexual and culinary enhancements; they come with the territory.  But there are many other ways in which cannabis can catalyze the enhancement of a variety of personal capacities. 

 

For example, it can catalyze new ideas and insights, heighten the appreciation of music and art, deepen emotional and sexual intimacy, and facilitate the depth of spiritual experiences, to name a few.  This capacity is often misunderstood or under-appreciated, not only by non-users, but even by some users, especially young people who are primarily interested in promoting sociability and fun. 

 

Most of marijuana’s powers of enhancement are not as immediately available as its capacity to lift mood, or improve appetite and the taste of food, and enhance sexual pleasure.  More experienced users appear to have a greater appreciation of this capacity.

 

(3) Medicine. When I first considered this issue in the early 1970s, I assumed that cannabis as medicine would be identical to the marijuana used for other purposes (the dried flowering tops of female Cannabis plants); its toxicity is minimal, its dosage is easily titrated when it is inhaled and, once freed of the prohibition tariff, it will be inexpensive. 

 

I thought the main problem was its classification in Schedule 1 of the Comprehensive Drug Abuse and Control Act of 1970, which describes it as having a high potential for abuse, no accepted medical use, and lack of accepted safety for use even under medical supervision. 

 

At that time I naïvely believed that a change to Schedule 2 would overcome a major obstacle to its legal availability as a medicine.  I thought that once it was transferred to Schedule 2, clinical research on herbal marijuana would eagerly be pursued. 

 

More than a third of a century later I have begun to doubt this.  I used to think that it would be highly desirable if marijuana could be approved as a legitimate medicine within the present federal regulatory system, but it now seems to me not only highly unlikely, but not even desirable. 

 

Today, transferring marijuana to Schedule 2 would not be enough to make it available as a prescription drug.  Such drugs must undergo rigorous, expensive, and time-consuming tests before they are approved by the FDA.  This system is designed to regulate the commercial distribution of drug company products and to protect the public against false or misleading claims about their efficacy and safety.  The drug is generally a single synthetic chemical that a pharmaceutical company has developed and patented. 

From 1998 See DEA FINALLY CONFIRMS THE EXISTENCE OF SUFFICIENT GROUNDS TO REMOVE MARIJUANA FROM HARD DRUGS SCHEDULE OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES

 

The company submits an application to the FDA and tests it first for safety in animals and then for clinical safety and efficiency.  The company must present evidence from double-blind controlled studies demonstrating that the drug is more effective than a placebo and as effective as available drugs.  Case reports, expert opinion, clinical experience and anecdotal evidence are not considered sufficient.  The cost of this evaluation exceeds $200 million per drug.

 

It is unlikely that whole smoked marijuana will ever be developed as an officially recognized medicine via this route.  Thousands of years of use have demonstrated its medical value; the extensive government supported effort of the last four decades to establish a sufficient level of toxicity to support the harsh prohibition has, instead, provided a record of safety that is far more compelling than that of nearly all medicines in the US pharmacopeia. 

 

The modern FDA protocol is not necessary to establish a risk-benefit estimate for marijuana with its long history as a safe medicine.  To impose this protocol on cannabis would be like making the same demand of aspirin, which was accepted as a medicine more than 60 years before the advent of the double-blind controlled study.  Many years of experience have shown us that aspirin has many uses and limited toxicity; yet today it could not be marshaled through the FDA approval process. 

 

The patent has long since expired, and with it the incentive to underwrite the enormous cost of this modern medical seal of approval.

 

But let us, for the moment, imagine that the government has granted  marijuana legitimacy as a medicine while continuing to prohibit it for the previously mentioned uses.  How would the appropriate "labeled" uses be determined and how would "off-label" uses be dealt with? 

 

Then there is the question who would supply the cannabis?  The federal government now provides marijuana from its farm in Mississippi to the few surviving patients of the long-discontinued Compassionate IND program.  But surely the government could not or would not produce marijuana for many thousands of patients receiving prescriptions, any more than it does for other prescription drugs.  If production is contracted out, will the growers have to enclose their fields with security fences and employ security guards?  How would marijuana be distributed?  If through pharmacies, how would they provide secure facilities capable of keeping fresh supplies? 

 

Would it offer a sufficient variety of different strains?  Would the price of pharmaceutical herbal marijuana have to be controlled: not too high, lest patients be tempted to buy it on the street or grow their own; not too low, lest people with marginal or completely fictitious "medical" conditions besiege their doctors for prescriptions because it is cheaper than what is being sold on the street?  What about the parallel problems with potency?  When urine tests are demanded for workers, how would those who use marijuana legally as a medicine be distinguished from those who use it for other purposes?

 

To realize the full potential of cannabis as a medicine in the setting of the present prohibition, we would have to address all these problems and more.  A delivery system that successfully navigated this minefield would be cumbersome, inefficient, and bureaucratically top-heavy.  Government and medical licensing boards would insist on tight control, challenging physicians as though cannabis were a dangerous drug every time it was used for any new patient or purpose.  There would be constant conflict with one of two outcomes; patients would not get all of the benefits they should, or they would get the benefits by abandoning the legal system for the black market or their own gardens and closets.

 

A solution to the medicine part of the prohibition proposed notably in the Institute of Medicine Report is what might be called the "pharmaceuticalization" of cannabis: prescription of isolated individual cannabinoids, synthetic cannabinoids and cannabinoid analogues.  The IOM Report states that "if there is any future for marijuana as a medicine, it lies in its isolated components, the cannabinoids, and their synthetic derivatives." 

 

It goes on: "Therefore, the purpose of clinical trials of smoked marijuana would not be to develop marijuana as a licensed drug, but such trials could be a first step towards the development of rapid-onset non-smoked delivery systems."  Now, some cannabinoids and analogues may have advantages over smoked or ingested marijuana in limited circumstances.  For example, cannabidiol may be more effective as an anti-anxiety medicine and an anti-convulsant when it is not taken along with tetrahydrocannabinol, which sometimes generates anxiety. 

 

Other cannabinoid analogues may occasionally prove more useful than marijuana because they can be administered intravenously.  I am prepared to believe that some synthetic analogues may offer medical advantages that we cannot now anticipate. The question is whether these developments will make herbal marijuana itself medically obsolete.  Surely many of these new products would be useful and safe enough for commercial development.  It is uncertain, however, whether pharmaceutical companies will find them worth the enormous developmental costs. 

 

Some may be; for example imagine that some pharmaceutical company develops an inverse munchies cannabinoid agonist that safely reduces appetite; might not that be highly lucrative? But for most specific symptoms, analogues or combinations of analogues are unlikely to be more useful than natural cannabis.  Nor are they likely to have a significantly wider spectrum of therapeutic uses, since the natural product contains all the compounds (and synergistic combinations of compounds) from which they are derived.  They could certainly never have a more favorable therapeutic ratio (that is be safer) than herbal marijuana.  In any event, pharmaceuticals will have to be ultimately tested against herbal marijuana because IT IS the medical gold standard. 

 

So far pharmaceutical companies have been unwilling to test their products against this standard.  I suspect it is because they would confirm my clinical experience with Marinol and Sativex; of the patients I am acquainted with who have had the opportunity to use, at different times, marijuana and one of these pharmaceuticals, not one has preferred the pharmaceutical.  Invariably they found marijuana to be more efficacious with fewer side effects and less expensive than the conventional medicine it replaced. I think the only thing these pharmaceuticals have going for them is that they are legal.

 

Since 1996 we have seen some compassionate reform with respect to the use of marijuana as a medicine in 14 states.  And there is little doubt that this has been a boon to many sick people in those states.  However, because each of those states narrowly define the symptoms and syndromes for which doctors can "prescribe" cannabis, only a fraction of patients who could take advantage of the wide range of its medicinal capacities are allowed to do so.  Furthermore, patients, caregivers, growers and compassion clubs have to endure constant conflict with federal authorities.

 

It now seems to me that it is hopeless to think that we can find a way to deliver herbal marijuana as a prescription medicine as long as it is outlawed for any other use.  What is even more important, I no longer think it makes sense to treat it as a prescription medicine, to continue to try to make it fit into this Procrustean bed.  It is now clear to the growing number of clinicians who have become familiar with its use as a medicine that it is safer than many, if not most, over-the-counter medicines, and it should be treated in the same fashion. 

 

A patient who has a common headache should be able to treat it with aspirin, ibuprofen or marijuana; the choice should be his.  What we have seen so far are minor reforms. The bottom line is that the marijuana prohibition, with all of its ugliness, must go.  This is the only way that adult citizens who wish to use this herb for any reason, recreation, personal enhancement, or as a medicine will be free to do so.  We don't want to have to continue to chip away with one little reform in one state at a time.  As with alcohol, “We want  repeal and we want it now.”
